evidence.quote: The increases in average price per ad in the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026 were driven by an increase in advertising demand, which we believe is mostly due to ongoing improvements to our ad targeting and measurement tools. A favorable foreign currency exchange impact also contributed to the increase in the nine months ended September 30, 2026. These increases were partially offset by a higher number of ad impressions delivered, especially in geographies and in products, such as Reels, that monetize at lower rates.

input.label: SUPPORTED
input.change_reason: Upon deeper analysis, the claim is SUPPORTED. The evidence shows that in Q3 2026, ad impressions increased 10% year-over-year while average price per ad increased 14% year-over-year (E3, E1). Mathematically, in a multiplicative revenue model (Revenue = Impressions × Price), the 14% price increase contributes more to the overall 26% revenue growth than the 10% impressions increase. While H3 reveals that mix effects and other factors influenced both metrics, this doesn't change the fundamental comparison: price per ad grew at a higher rate (14%) than impressions (10%), meaning price was the larger driver of revenue growth. The filing states revenue was driven by "increases in ad impressions delivered and average price per ad" (E3) but doesn't explicitly rank them; however, the numerical evidence clearly shows price increased more in percentage terms, supporting the claim that growth was driven MORE by price than by impressions.

supporting_evidence.quote: Advertising revenue in the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026 increased $12.98 billion, or 26%, and $39.41 billion, or 29%, respectively, compared to the same periods in 2025, due to increases in ad impressions delivered and average price per ad. During the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026, ad impressions delivered increased by 10% and 14%, respectively, year-over-year
During the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026, the average price per ad increased by 14% and 13%, respectively, year-over-year
Ad impressions delivered across our Family of Apps in the third quarter of 2026 increased 10% year-over-year, and our average price per ad in the third quarter of 2026 increased 14% year-over-year.

input.reasoning_summary: The claim states that Meta's advertising revenue growth in Q3 2026 was driven more by higher average price per ad than by more ad impressions. The evidence clearly establishes: (1) Ad impressions increased 10% YoY in Q3 2026, (2) Average price per ad increased 14% YoY in Q3 2026, and (3) Advertising revenue increased 26% YoY. In a multiplicative revenue model where Revenue = Impressions × Price, the approximate contribution is (1.10) × (1.14) ≈ 1.254 or ~25.4% growth, consistent with the reported 26%. When comparing the relative drivers, the 14% price increase is larger than the 10% impressions increase, meaning price per ad was indeed the larger driver. While H3 identified that mix effects (geographic mix, Reels monetization) and currency impacts affected these metrics, this doesn't contradict the claim—it explains WHY the metrics moved as they did. The claim is about which factor contributed MORE, and the evidence supports that price (14% growth) contributed more than impressions (10% growth).
